title: Steve Kemboi
text:
I study how to price financial and insurance risk when we are not sure our model is right.
Most pricing models assume we know their parameters exactly: how fast interest rates pull back to normal, how volatile a currency is. In practice, those numbers are estimated from noisy data and they drift over time. My research asks a simple question:
I work with nonlinear affine processes, a framework that keeps the tractability of classic models such as Cox–Ingersoll–Ross while letting the parameters be uncertain. I apply it to currency options and weather derivatives.
I am advised by Dr. Tolulope Fadina at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Before UIUC I trained at AIMS (University of Cape Town) and Michigan State University (M.S. Industrial Mathematics).
More about my research →

title: Pricing currency options when the model is uncertain
text: In Part 2 we priced bonds when the interest-rate model’s parameters were only known to lie in a box. Now we move to the application at the centre of my current project: currency (FX) options.

title: Pricing currency options when the model is uncertain
section: Step 1 · What is a currency option?
text:
Step 1 · What is a currency option?
A US company will receive €1 million in a year. If the euro weakens, it loses money in dollar terms. It can protect itself with an FX option.
A call on EUR/USD with strike K gives the right, not the obligation, to buy €1 at K dollars at time T. If the exchange rate ends at S_T, the payoff is

\text{payoff} = \max(S_T - K,\ 0).



Show the code
S = np.linspace(0.9, 1.3, 400); K = 1.10
plt.plot(S, np.maximum(S - K, 0), color=NAVY, lw=2.2, label="call: max(S − K, 0)")
plt.plot(S, np.maximum(K - S, 0), color=ORANGE, lw=2.2, label="put: max(K − S, 0)")
plt.axvline(K, color="k", ls=":", lw=1); plt.text(K, .19, " strike K = 1.10")
plt.xlabel("EUR/USD at maturity ($ per €)"); plt.ylabel("payoff ($ per €)"); plt.legend(); plt.show()








Figure 1: Payoffs at maturity, per €1: a call (right to buy euros at K = 1.10) and a put (right to sell). The option is worth exercising only on one side of the strike.

title: Pricing currency options when the model is uncertain
section: Step 2 · Why FX is different: two interest rates
text:
Step 2 · Why FX is different: two interest rates
Holding euros earns the euro interest rate r_f (foreign), while dollars earn the dollar rate r_d (domestic). A currency therefore behaves like a stock that pays a continuous dividend r_f. Under the pricing measure the exchange rate follows

dS_t = (r_d - r_f)\,S_t\,dt + \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t .

With constant r_d, r_f, \sigma this gives the Garman–Kohlhagen (1983) formula, the Black–Scholes formula for currencies:

C = S_0 e^{-r_f T}\,N(d_1) - K e^{-r_d T}\,N(d_2), \qquad d_{1,2} = \frac{\ln(S_0/K) + (r_d - r_f \pm \tfrac12\sigma^2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T}.



Show the code
def gk_call(S, K, T, rd, rf, sig):
    d1 = (np.log(S / K) + (rd - rf + 0.5 * sig**2) * T) / (sig * np.sqrt(T)); d2 = d1 - sig * np.sqrt(T)
    return S * np.exp(-rf * T) * norm.cdf(d1) - K * np.exp(-rd * T) * norm.cdf(d2)

rd, rf, T = 0.045, 0.025, 1.0
for sig, c in [(0.06, TEAL), (0.09, NAVY), (0.12, ORANGE)]:
    plt.plot(S, gk_call(S, K, T, rd, rf, sig), color=c, lw=2, label=f"σ = {sig:.0%}")
plt.plot(S, np.maximum(S - K, 0), "k:", lw=1, label="payoff")
plt.xlabel("EUR/USD today"); plt.ylabel("call price ($ per €)"); plt.legend(); plt.show()








Figure 2: Garman–Kohlhagen call prices one year before maturity for three volatilities (r_d = 4.5%, r_f = 2.5%). Higher volatility means a more valuable option, because the upside is unlimited while the downside is capped at zero.

title: Pricing currency options when the model is uncertain
section: Step 3 · Where my project starts
text:
Step 3 · Where my project starts
Garman–Kohlhagen assumes constant rates and volatility. Real FX markets violate both: volatility clusters and moves randomly, and both interest rates move. Classic work by Melino & Turnbull (1991) moved toward stochastic volatility for currency options. My project asks the next question: the volatility and rate dynamics themselves have uncertain parameters, so we model them with the nonlinear CIR family from Part 2 and look for price bounds.
To see the main effect clearly, this post isolates one ingredient: volatility known only to lie in a range \sigma \in [\underline\sigma, \overline\sigma], possibly changing over time. Here we use [6\%, 12\%].

title: Pricing currency options when the model is uncertain
section: Step 4 · Easy case: a plain call
text:
Step 4 · Easy case: a plain call
The robust upper price is the supremum over all volatility paths in the band. By the same dynamic-programming argument as in Part 2, it solves a nonlinear PDE, the Black–Scholes–Barenblatt equation (Avellaneda, Levy & Parás 1995):

\partial_t V + \tfrac12\,\Sigma(\Gamma)^2 S^2\,\partial_{SS}V + (r_d - r_f) S\,\partial_S V - r_d V = 0,
\qquad
\Sigma(\Gamma) = \begin{cases}\overline\sigma & \Gamma = \partial_{SS}V \ge 0\\ \underline\sigma & \Gamma < 0\end{cases}

(for the lower price, swap the roles of \overline\sigma and \underline\sigma). Nature picks high volatility wherever the option is convex and low volatility wherever it is concave.
A call is convex everywhere, so the upper price is just Garman–Kohlhagen at \overline\sigma and the lower is GK at \underline\sigma. This is the same “corner” story as the bond in Part 2.


Show the code
def bsb(payoff, S0grid, T, rd, rf, slo, shi, upper=True, nx=600, dt=2e-4):
    """Black–Scholes–Barenblatt in log-spot, explicit finite differences."""
    x = np.linspace(np.log(0.6), np.log(1.9), nx); dx = x[1] - x[0]
    V = payoff(np.exp(x))
    for _ in range(int(T / dt)):
        Vx = np.gradient(V, dx); Vxx = np.zeros(nx); Vxx[1:-1] = (V[2:] - 2 * V[1:-1] + V[:-2]) / dx**2
        gamma = Vxx - Vx                                   # sign of S² ∂_SS V
        sig = np.where(gamma >= 0, shi, slo) if upper else np.where(gamma >= 0, slo, shi)
        V = V + dt * (0.5 * sig**2 * (Vxx - Vx) + (rd - rf) * Vx - rd * V)
        V[0] = 2 * V[1] - V[2]; V[-1] = 2 * V[-2] - V[-3]
    return np.interp(np.log(S0grid), x, V)

slo, shi = 0.06, 0.12
call = lambda s: np.maximum(s - K, 0)




Show the code
S0 = np.linspace(0.95, 1.25, 120)
up, dn = bsb(call, S0, T, rd, rf, slo, shi, True), bsb(call, S0, T, rd, rf, slo, shi, False)
plt.fill_between(S0, dn, up, color=ORANGE, alpha=.25, label="robust band (PDE)")
plt.plot(S0, gk_call(S0, K, T, rd, rf, shi), "--", color=ORANGE, lw=1.6, label="GK at σ = 12%")
plt.plot(S0, gk_call(S0, K, T, rd, rf, slo), "--", color=TEAL, lw=1.6, label="GK at σ = 6%")
plt.xlabel("EUR/USD today"); plt.ylabel("call price ($ per €)"); plt.legend(); plt.show()








Figure 3: Robust bounds for the call (shaded, computed by the nonlinear PDE) line up exactly with Garman–Kohlhagen at the edges of the volatility band (dashed).

title: Pricing currency options when the model is uncertain
section: Step 5 · Interesting case: a butterfly spread
text:
Step 5 · Interesting case: a butterfly spread
Now take a payoff that is convex in some places and concave in others. A butterfly (long a 1.00 call, short two 1.10 calls, long a 1.20 call) pays off if the euro ends up near 1.10. Exporters use structures like this when they expect a stable exchange rate.
For such a payoff nature’s worst choice of volatility switches with the state: high where the price is convex (the wings) and low where it is concave (near 1.10). No single constant volatility reproduces this.


Show the code
K1, K2, K3 = 1.00, 1.10, 1.20
fly = lambda s: np.maximum(s - K1, 0) - 2 * np.maximum(s - K2, 0) + np.maximum(s - K3, 0)
fly_gk = lambda s, sig: gk_call(s, K1, T, rd, rf, sig) - 2 * gk_call(s, K2, T, rd, rf, sig) + gk_call(s, K3, T, rd, rf, sig)

up, dn = bsb(fly, S0, T, rd, rf, slo, shi, True), bsb(fly, S0, T, rd, rf, slo, shi, False)
const = np.array([fly_gk(S0, s) for s in np.linspace(slo, shi, 25)])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.6]})
Sp = np.linspace(0.9, 1.3, 400)
axes[0].plot(Sp, fly(Sp), color=NAVY, lw=2.2); axes[0].set_title("payoff at maturity")
axes[0].set_xlabel("EUR/USD at maturity"); axes[0].set_ylabel("$ per €")

axes[1].fill_between(S0, dn, up, color=ORANGE, alpha=.25, label="robust band (PDE)")
for c in const: axes[1].plot(S0, c, color=NAVY, alpha=.25, lw=.8)
axes[1].plot([], [], color=NAVY, alpha=.5, label="constant σ ∈ [6%, 12%]")
j = np.argmin(abs(S0 - 1.10))
axes[1].annotate("", xy=(1.10, up[j]), xytext=(1.10, const.max(0)[j]), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#be123c", lw=1.6))
axes[1].annotate("", xy=(1.10, dn[j]), xytext=(1.10, const.min(0)[j]), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#be123c", lw=1.6))
axes[1].set_title("price one year before maturity"); axes[1].set_xlabel("EUR/USD today"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"At S = 1.10: constant-σ prices span {const.min(0)[j]:.4f}–{const.max(0)[j]:.4f};"
      f" robust range is {dn[j]:.4f}–{up[j]:.4f} ($ per €)")








Figure 4: Butterfly spread. Thin lines: Garman–Kohlhagen prices for 25 constant volatilities between 6% and 12%. Shaded: the robust band from the nonlinear PDE, which is strictly wider than the envelope of all constant-volatility prices (red arrows).





At S = 1.10: constant-σ prices span 0.0275–0.0472; robust range is 0.0193–0.0531 ($ per €)


What to notice: the robust band is visibly wider than anything you get by trying constant volatilities one at a time. A trader who stress-tests by “re-running the model at 6% and at 12%” would underestimate model risk on this product. The robust price is what it actually costs to hedge safely when the volatility could be anywhere in the band.

title: Pricing currency options when the model is uncertain
section: Step 6 · Where this is going
text:
Step 6 · Where this is going


Show the code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 2.6)); ax.axis("off"); ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 3)
boxes = [(0.2, "Constant σ, r_d, r_f\n(Garman–Kohlhagen)", "white"),
         (2.7, "σ in a band\n(BSB equation)\nthis post", "#fde7d3"),
         (5.2, "σ² follows nonlinear\nCIR (Heston-type)", "white"),
         (7.7, "σ², r_d, r_f all\nnonlinear CIR", "white")]
for xb, txt, fc in boxes:
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((xb, .7), 2.1, 1.6, fc=fc, ec=NAVY, lw=1.5, zorder=2))
    ax.text(xb + 1.05, 1.5, txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9.5, zorder=3)
for xb in [2.3, 4.8, 7.3]:
    ax.annotate("", xy=(xb + .4, 1.5), xytext=(xb, 1.5), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=ORANGE, lw=2))
plt.show()








Figure 5: The pieces of the project. This post covered the shaded box; the full model lets the volatility and both interest rates follow nonlinear CIR dynamics.





The next steps replace the simple volatility band with the nonlinear CIR family of Part 2, applied to the variance (a robust Heston model) and to both interest rates. Prices are still computed from nonlinear PDEs, but now in several dimensions, which raises real numerical questions. Later posts will cover those, along with how to estimate the uncertainty box from market data.

Recap, step by step. FX option payoff (Step 1) → two interest rates and the Garman–Kohlhagen formula (Step 2) → uncertainty in the volatility (Step 3) → for convex payoffs the bounds sit at the edges of the band (Step 4) → for mixed payoffs the robust band is strictly wider than any constant-parameter stress test (Step 5).
The lesson of the series: when parameters are uncertain, “try a few values” is not enough. The right answer comes from a nonlinear expectation, and affine structure is what keeps it computable.

Previous: Part 2
References. Garman & Kohlhagen (1983), Journal of International Money and Finance · Avellaneda, Levy & Parás (1995), Applied Mathematical Finance · Melino & Turnbull (1991), Canadian Journal of Economics · Fadina, Neufeld & Schmidt (2019), Probability, Uncertainty and Quantitative Risk.

title: Research
text: A pricing model is a machine. Feed it parameters and it returns a price. The trouble is that the parameters are estimates, and small changes in them can move the price a lot. Robust pricing replaces the single number with an interval of prices: the cheapest and the most expensive values consistent with everything we believe about the parameters.

title: Research
section: 1. Nonlinear affine processes
text:
1. Nonlinear affine processes
Affine models such as Vasicek, Cox–Ingersoll–Ross (CIR) and Heston are the workhorses of interest-rate and volatility modelling because their prices come in near closed form. Fadina, Neufeld & Schmidt (2019) showed how to keep that structure while letting the drift and volatility parameters move inside an uncertainty set. Prices then come from a nonlinear expectation, the worst or best case over all admissible parameter paths.
Questions I work on: how to estimate the uncertainty set from data, how to check the nonlinear Feller condition (which keeps rates positive), and how to compute the price bounds efficiently.
Start here: Post 1 · Post 2

title: Research
section: 2. Robust currency option pricing
text:
2. Robust currency option pricing
A currency option depends on two interest rates (domestic and foreign) and on the exchange-rate volatility. My current project builds on the stochastic-volatility FX option literature, starting from Melino & Turnbull (1991), and recasts it in the nonlinear CIR framework. The goal is option price bounds that stay honest about parameter uncertainty.
Start here: Post 3

title: Research
section: 3. Weather derivatives
text:
3. Weather derivatives
Temperature-based contracts (heating and cooling degree-day options) protect farms, utilities and insurers against weather risk. Temperature models are mean-reverting and seasonal, and their parameters are very uncertain, which makes them a natural next application of the same robust machinery.

Methods and tools
Stochastic calculus · nonlinear (sublinear) expectations · HJB / Black–Scholes–Barenblatt PDEs · Fourier pricing (Gil-Pelaez inversion) · maximum-likelihood estimation with constraints · Python, R, MATLAB.

title: What if we don’t know the parameters?
text:
In Part 1 we built the CIR model
dr_t = \kappa(\theta - r_t)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r_t}\,dW_t
and treated \kappa (speed of pull), \theta (long-run level) and \sigma (noise) as known. In practice we estimate them from data. This post asks how much those estimates can be trusted, and what to do when they can’t.

title: What if we don’t know the parameters?
section: Step 1 · Estimate the parameters, then do it again 1,000 times
text:
Step 1 · Estimate the parameters, then do it again 1,000 times
Let’s play a game where we know the truth. We simulate 10 years of monthly interest rates from a CIR model with \kappa = 0.5, \theta = 3\%, \sigma = 0.09, then estimate the parameters from that data the way a practitioner would. Then we repeat with 1,000 fresh data sets.
The estimator divides the discretized model by \sqrt{r_t} so it becomes an ordinary linear regression:

\frac{r_{t+\Delta}-r_t}{\sqrt{r_t}} = \kappa\theta\,\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{r_t}} - \kappa\,\sqrt{r_t}\,\Delta + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta}\,\varepsilon_t .



Show the code
def sim_cir(kappa, theta, sigma, r0, n, dt, sub=20):
    h = dt / sub; r = np.empty(n + 1); r[0] = r0; x = r0
    for k in range(n):
        for _ in range(sub):
            xp = max(x, 0); x = x + kappa * (theta - xp) * h + sigma * np.sqrt(xp * h) * rng.standard_normal()
        r[k + 1] = max(x, 1e-6)
    return r

def ols_cir(r, dt):
    y = (r[1:] - r[:-1]) / np.sqrt(r[:-1])
    X = np.column_stack([dt / np.sqrt(r[:-1]), np.sqrt(r[:-1]) * dt])
    b, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
    kappa = -b[1]; theta = b[0] / kappa
    sigma = np.std(y - X @ b, ddof=2) / np.sqrt(dt)
    return kappa, theta, sigma

true = dict(kappa=0.5, theta=0.03, sigma=0.09)
est = np.array([ols_cir(sim_cir(**true, r0=0.03, n=120, dt=1/12), 1/12) for _ in range(1000)])
ok = (est[:, 0] > 0) & (est[:, 1] > 0) & (est[:, 1] < 0.2)
est = est[ok]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
axes[0].hist(est[:, 0], bins=50, color=NAVY, alpha=.75); axes[0].axvline(true["kappa"], color=ORANGE, ls="--", lw=2)
axes[0].set_xlabel("estimated κ (speed of mean reversion)")
axes[1].hist(100 * est[:, 1], bins=50, range=(0, 8), color=TEAL, alpha=.75); axes[1].axvline(100 * true["theta"], color=ORANGE, ls="--", lw=2)
axes[1].set_xlabel("estimated θ (long-run level, %)")
for ax in axes: ax.set_ylabel("count")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
q = np.percentile(est[:, 0], [5, 95])
print(f"90% of κ-estimates lie between {q[0]:.2f} and {q[1]:.2f} (truth 0.50)")








Figure 1: Estimates of κ and θ from 1,000 independent 10-year monthly samples of the same CIR model. The dashed lines show the truth. Even with a decade of data, the middle 90% of κ-estimates span roughly a factor of six.





90% of κ-estimates lie between 0.30 and 1.86 (truth 0.50)


What to notice: the speed of mean reversion \kappa is notoriously hard to pin down, and its estimates are biased upward. The long-run level \theta is also very uncertain. This is not bad statistics; ten years is simply not that much information about a slow process.

title: What if we don’t know the parameters?
section: Step 2 · Two ways to respond
text:
Step 2 · Two ways to respond
Classical approach: take the point estimate, plug it in, and price. One number, but it hides the uncertainty from Step 1.
Robust approach: admit that the parameters lie somewhere in a range, and possibly even change over time inside that range. Write the CIR drift as b_0 + b_1 r (so b_0=\kappa\theta, b_1=-\kappa) and the squared noise as a = \sigma^2, and allow

b_0 \in [\underline b_0, \overline b_0], \qquad b_1 \in [\underline b_1, \overline b_1], \qquad a \in [\underline a, \overline a].

The rate now follows

dr_t = (b_0(t) + b_1(t)\, r_t)\,dt + \sqrt{a(t)\, r_t}\; dW_t,

where the parameter paths b_0(t), b_1(t), a(t) are unknown and can be any (adapted) choice inside the box. This is a nonlinear affine process, the framework of Fadina, Neufeld & Schmidt (2019). It is not one model but a whole family of models, and we want answers that hold for all of them.


Show the code
lo = dict(b0=0.012, b1=-0.7, a=0.07**2); hi = dict(b0=0.018, b1=-0.3, a=0.11**2)
T, n = 10, 2400; dt = T / n; t = np.linspace(0, T, n + 1); dW = rng.standard_normal(n) * np.sqrt(dt)

def path(rule):
    r = np.empty(n + 1); r[0] = 0.03
    for k in range(n):
        b0, b1, a = rule(k, r[k]); rp = max(r[k], 0)
        r[k + 1] = r[k] + (b0 + b1 * rp) * dt + np.sqrt(a * rp) * dW[k]
    return 100 * np.maximum(r, 0)

mid = lambda k, r: (0.015, -0.5, 0.09**2)
switch_year = lambda k, r: (hi["b0"], hi["b1"], hi["a"]) if (k * dt) % 2 < 1 else (lo["b0"], lo["b1"], lo["a"])
adversarial = lambda k, r: (hi["b0"], hi["b1"], hi["a"]) if r > 0.03 else (lo["b0"], lo["b1"], lo["a"])
rand_reg = np.repeat(rng.integers(0, 2, n // 120 + 1), 120)
random_regime = lambda k, r: tuple((hi if rand_reg[k] else lo)[p] for p in ("b0", "b1", "a"))

plt.plot(t, path(mid), color=NAVY, lw=2, label="fixed parameters")
plt.plot(t, path(switch_year), color=ORANGE, lw=1, label="switches every year")
plt.plot(t, path(adversarial), color=TEAL, lw=1, label="depends on the rate level")
plt.plot(t, path(random_regime), color=GREY, lw=1, label="random regimes")
plt.xlabel("years"); plt.ylabel("interest rate (%)"); plt.legend(fontsize=9, ncol=2); plt.show()








Figure 2: One fixed CIR model (navy) versus three members of the nonlinear CIR family, whose parameters switch within the uncertainty box over time (orange, teal, grey). All use the same random shocks.











NoteThe nonlinear Feller condition



In Part 1 we needed 2\kappa\theta \ge \sigma^2 to keep the rate positive. Now it must hold for every model in the family, and the worst case is the weakest pull with the strongest noise: 2\underline b_0 \ge \overline a. Here 2(0.012) = 0.024 \ge 0.0121, so it holds.

title: What if we don’t know the parameters?
section: Step 3 · Price a bond for each fixed parameter
text:
Step 3 · Price a bond for each fixed parameter
A zero-coupon bond pays $1 at time T. Its price today is the expected discount factor \mathbb E\big[e^{-\int_0^T r_s\,ds}\big]. CIR is an affine model, which means this price has a closed form:

P(T) = A(T)\, e^{-B(T)\, r_0},

with explicit A and B. That is the “affine” in “affine processes”: the log price is linear in the current rate. It is what makes these models so practical.


Show the code
def cir_bond(b0, b1, a, r0, tau):
    kappa = -b1; theta = b0 / kappa; g = np.sqrt(kappa**2 + 2 * a)
    e = np.exp(g * tau) - 1; den = (g + kappa) * e + 2 * g
    B = 2 * e / den; A = (2 * g * np.exp((kappa + g) * tau / 2) / den) ** (2 * kappa * theta / a)
    return A * np.exp(-B * r0)

tau = np.linspace(0.05, 10, 200); r0 = 0.03
for _ in range(200):
    b0, b1, a = [rng.uniform(lo[p], hi[p]) for p in ("b0", "b1", "a")]
    plt.plot(tau, -100 * np.log(cir_bond(b0, b1, a, r0, tau)) / tau, color=NAVY, alpha=.07)
plt.plot(tau, -100 * np.log(cir_bond(0.015, -0.5, 0.09**2, r0, tau)) / tau, color=ORANGE, lw=2.2, label="point estimate")
plt.xlabel("maturity (years)"); plt.ylabel("yield (%)"); plt.legend(); plt.show()








Figure 3: Yield curves from the CIR closed form for 200 random fixed parameter choices inside the uncertainty box. Each curve is a perfectly reasonable model, and they disagree strongly at long maturities.

title: What if we don’t know the parameters?
section: Step 4 · The robust price: best and worst case over the whole family
text:
Step 4 · The robust price: best and worst case over the whole family
The robust upper price is the highest value any model in the family can produce, including models whose parameters change over time and react to the market:

\overline P(T) = \sup_{\text{parameter paths in the box}} \mathbb E\Big[e^{-\int_0^T r_s\,ds}\Big],

and the lower price \underline P(T) is the infimum. This is a nonlinear expectation. It is no longer linear in the payoff, which is where the name nonlinear affine process comes from.
How do we compute a supremum over infinitely many parameter paths? Dynamic programming turns it into a PDE in which, at every point, nature picks the worst parameters:

\partial_\tau u = \sup_{b_0,b_1}\,(b_0 + b_1 x)\,\partial_x u \;+\; \sup_{a}\, \tfrac12\, a\, x\, \partial_{xx} u \;-\; x\,u, \qquad u(0,x)=1 .

Each \sup is easy: it just picks an endpoint of the interval depending on the sign of \partial_x u or \partial_{xx} u. We solve it with finite differences.


Show the code
def robust_bond(lo, hi, T, upper=True, xmax=0.30, nx=151, dt=4e-4):
    x = np.linspace(0, xmax, nx); dx = x[1] - x[0]; u = np.ones(nx)
    out = [(0.0, u.copy())]; steps = int(T / dt)
    for k in range(steps):
        ux_f = np.r_[(u[1:] - u[:-1]) / dx, 0]; ux_b = np.r_[0, (u[1:] - u[:-1]) / dx]
        uxx = np.zeros(nx); uxx[1:-1] = (u[2:] - 2 * u[1:-1] + u[:-2]) / dx**2
        pick = (lambda s: s > 0) if upper else (lambda s: s < 0)
        ux_c = np.gradient(u, dx)
        b0 = np.where(pick(ux_c), hi["b0"], lo["b0"]); b1 = np.where(pick(x * ux_c), hi["b1"], lo["b1"])
        a = np.where(pick(uxx), hi["a"], lo["a"])
        drift = b0 + b1 * x
        ux = np.where(drift > 0, ux_f, ux_b)          # upwinding
        u = u + dt * (drift * ux + 0.5 * a * x * uxx - x * u)
        u[-1] = 2 * u[-2] - u[-3]                      # linear extrapolation at the far boundary
        out.append(((k + 1) * dt, u.copy()))
    return x, out

mats = np.linspace(0, 10, 41)
x, up = robust_bond(lo, hi, 10, upper=True); _, dn = robust_bond(lo, hi, 10, upper=False)
i0 = np.argmin(abs(x - 0.03)); times = np.array([s for s, _ in up])
U = np.array([up[np.argmin(abs(times - m))][1][i0] for m in mats]); L = np.array([dn[np.argmin(abs(times - m))][1][i0] for m in mats])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 6.4), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2.2, 1]})
axes[0].fill_between(mats, L, U, color=ORANGE, alpha=.25, label="robust band (nonlinear PDE)")
for _ in range(200):
    b0, b1, a = [rng.uniform(lo[p], hi[p]) for p in ("b0", "b1", "a")]
    axes[0].plot(tau, cir_bond(b0, b1, a, 0.03, tau), color=NAVY, alpha=.05)
axes[0].plot(tau, cir_bond(0.015, -0.5, 0.09**2, 0.03, tau), color=NAVY, lw=2, label="point estimate")
axes[0].set_ylabel("bond price ($)"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].plot(mats, 100 * (U - L), color=ORANGE, lw=2, label="width of robust band")
axes[1].plot(tau, 100 * (cir_bond(lo["b0"], lo["b1"], hi["a"], .03, tau) - cir_bond(hi["b0"], hi["b1"], lo["a"], .03, tau)),
             "k--", lw=1, label="corner closed forms")
axes[1].set_xlabel("maturity (years)"); axes[1].set_ylabel("cents per $1"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"10-year bond: point estimate ${cir_bond(0.015,-0.5,0.09**2,.03,10):.4f}, robust range ${L[-1]:.4f} – ${U[-1]:.4f}")








Figure 4: Robust bond-price bounds from the nonlinear PDE (shaded band) with the 200 fixed-parameter prices inside it. Lower panel: the PDE solution coincides with the closed-form price at the extreme ‘corner’ parameters.





10-year bond: point estimate $0.7433, robust range $0.6077 – $0.8288


What to notice:

The robust band contains every fixed-parameter price, and it widens quickly with maturity. For a 10-year bond the band is about 22 cents per dollar of face value: pure model risk.
For a bond the worst case happens at a corner of the box (weakest drift and strongest noise for the upper price), so the PDE agrees with the closed form at those corners. That is because the bond price is monotone and convex in the rate.
For contracts whose payoff is not monotone or convex, nature’s worst choice switches from one corner to another depending on the state, and no single fixed parameter gives the right bound. That is exactly what we will see with currency options in Part 3.


Recap, step by step. Estimates are uncertain (Step 1) → replace one parameter by a box (Step 2) → affine models still price each fixed model in closed form (Step 3) → the robust price is a sup/inf over the family, computed from a nonlinear PDE (Step 4).
Next: the same idea applied to currency options, where the payoff shape makes the robust answer genuinely different from any single model.

Previous: Part 1 · Next: Part 3 · Pricing currency options under uncertainty
Reference: T. Fadina, A. Neufeld, T. Schmidt (2019). Affine processes under parameter uncertainty. Probability, Uncertainty and Quantitative Risk 4:5.

title: From coin flips to the CIR model
text: My research is about pricing when we are unsure of a model’s parameters. Before we can be unsure of a model, we need a model. This first post builds one of the most important models in finance, the Cox–Ingersoll–Ross (CIR) model, from scratch. Each step adds exactly one idea.

title: From coin flips to the CIR model
section: Step 1 · A coin decides where we go
text:
Step 1 · A coin decides where we go
Flip a fair coin. Heads: move up one step. Tails: move down one step. Repeat. This is a random walk, the simplest model of something that changes unpredictably.


Show the code
n = 100
for i in range(5):
    steps = rng.choice([-1, 1], size=n)
    plt.plot(np.r_[0, steps.cumsum()], lw=1.6, color=[NAVY, ORANGE, TEAL, GREY, "#7c3aed"][i])
plt.axhline(0, color="k", lw=.8)
plt.xlabel("flip number"); plt.ylabel("position")
plt.show()








Figure 1: Five random walks of 100 coin flips each. No two paths look alike, but all of them wander with no tendency to return to zero.





What to notice: the paths drift further and further from zero as time passes. Their typical distance grows like the square root of the number of flips.

title: From coin flips to the CIR model
section: Step 2 · Make the steps tiny: Brownian motion
text:
Step 2 · Make the steps tiny: Brownian motion
Real prices and rates do not jump in whole units once a day. They move continuously. So we take smaller and smaller steps, more and more often, and shrink the step size like \sqrt{\Delta t} so the wiggle per unit of time stays fixed. In the limit we get Brownian motion W_t, the basic building block of stochastic calculus.


Show the code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.3), sharey=True)
z = rng.standard_normal(10_000)
for ax, n in zip(axes, [10, 100, 10_000]):
    dt = 1 / n
    incr = z[: n] * np.sqrt(dt) if n == 10_000 else z.reshape(n, -1).sum(1) * np.sqrt(1 / 10_000)
    ax.plot(np.linspace(0, 1, n + 1), np.r_[0, incr.cumsum()], color=NAVY, lw=1.2)
    ax.set_title(f"{n:,} steps"); ax.set_xlabel("time")
axes[0].set_ylabel("$W_t$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Figure 2: As the step size shrinks (10, 100, then 10,000 steps over the same time interval), the random walk converges to a continuous but very rough path: Brownian motion.





In shorthand, a tiny change of Brownian motion over a tiny time dt is written dW_t. It is random, has mean zero and variance dt.

title: From coin flips to the CIR model
section: Step 3 · Interest rates come back home: mean reversion
text:
Step 3 · Interest rates come back home: mean reversion
Brownian motion is a poor model of interest rates. Rates do not wander off forever: when they are unusually high, central banks and markets push them down, and when they are low, they drift up. We add a pull toward a long-run level \theta, with strength \kappa:

dr_t = \underbrace{\kappa(\theta - r_t)\,dt}_{\text{pull toward }\theta} + \underbrace{\sigma\, dW_t}_{\text{random shock}}

This is the Vasicek model (1977). When r_t > \theta the pull is negative and drags the rate down; when r_t<\theta it pushes up.


Show the code
kappa, theta, sigma, r0, T, n = 0.8, 0.03, 0.03, 0.08, 10, 2000
dt = T / n; t = np.linspace(0, T, n + 1)
for i, c in enumerate([NAVY, ORANGE, TEAL, GREY, "#7c3aed", "#be123c"]):
    r = np.empty(n + 1); r[0] = r0 if i < 3 else 0.0
    for k in range(n):
        r[k + 1] = r[k] + kappa * (theta - r[k]) * dt + sigma * np.sqrt(dt) * rng.standard_normal()
    plt.plot(t, 100 * r, color=c, lw=1.1)
plt.axhline(100 * theta, ls="--", color="k", lw=1); plt.text(T, 100 * theta + .2, " θ", va="bottom")
plt.axhspan(-10, 0, color="#fee2e2", zorder=-1); plt.ylim(-4, 9)
plt.xlabel("years"); plt.ylabel("interest rate (%)"); plt.show()








Figure 3: Vasicek paths start far from the long-run level θ = 3% and are pulled back toward it. But some paths fall below zero (shaded area).





What to notice: mean reversion works, but the random shock has the same size \sigma no matter how low the rate is, so rates can go negative. For many applications (and for modelling volatility, which can never be negative) that is a problem.

title: From coin flips to the CIR model
section: Step 4 · Shrink the noise near zero: the CIR model
text:
Step 4 · Shrink the noise near zero: the CIR model
Cox, Ingersoll and Ross (1985) made one small change: they scaled the shock by \sqrt{r_t}.

\boxed{\,dr_t = \kappa(\theta - r_t)\,dt + \sigma \sqrt{r_t}\, dW_t\,}

Now as the rate approaches zero the randomness fades away, while the pull \kappa\theta>0 keeps pushing upward. The rate cannot cross below zero.


Show the code
sigma_c = 0.12
paths = []
for i, c in enumerate([NAVY, ORANGE, TEAL, GREY, "#7c3aed", "#be123c"]):
    r = np.empty(n + 1); r[0] = r0 if i < 3 else 0.005
    for k in range(n):
        rp = max(r[k], 0.0)               # "full truncation" Euler scheme
        r[k + 1] = r[k] + kappa * (theta - rp) * dt + sigma_c * np.sqrt(rp * dt) * rng.standard_normal()
    plt.plot(t, 100 * np.maximum(r, 0), color=c, lw=1.1)
plt.axhline(100 * theta, ls="--", color="k", lw=1); plt.text(T, 100 * theta + .2, " θ", va="bottom")
plt.axhspan(-10, 0, color="#fee2e2", zorder=-1); plt.ylim(-4, 9)
plt.xlabel("years"); plt.ylabel("interest rate (%)"); plt.show()








Figure 4: CIR paths with the same κ, θ as before. The noise is large when rates are high and quiet near zero, so every path stays non-negative.

title: From coin flips to the CIR model
section: Step 5 · Can the rate touch zero? The Feller condition
text:
Step 5 · Can the rate touch zero? The Feller condition
Positivity has one more subtlety. If the noise \sigma is large compared with the upward pull \kappa\theta, the rate can still touch zero (and bounce back). It stays strictly positive exactly when

2\kappa\theta \;\ge\; \sigma^2 \qquad\text{(the Feller condition).}



Show the code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.5), sharey=True)
for ax, s, title in [(axes[0], 0.12, "Feller holds"), (axes[1], 0.40, "Feller fails")]:
    r = np.empty(n + 1); r[0] = 0.03
    for k in range(n):
        rp = max(r[k], 0.0)
        r[k + 1] = r[k] + kappa * (theta - rp) * dt + s * np.sqrt(rp * dt) * rng.standard_normal()
    ax.plot(t, 100 * np.maximum(r, 0), color=NAVY if s < .2 else ORANGE, lw=1)
    ax.set_title(f"{title}: σ = {s}"); ax.set_xlabel("years")
axes[0].set_ylabel("interest rate (%)"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Figure 5: Left: Feller condition holds (2κθ = 0.048 > σ² = 0.0144); the path stays away from zero. Right: it fails (2κθ = 0.048 < σ² = 0.16); the path repeatedly hits zero.





This condition will come back in Post 2, where the parameters are uncertain and we need it to hold for every admissible parameter, not just one.

title: From coin flips to the CIR model
section: Step 6 · Checking our simulation against the exact answer
text:
Step 6 · Checking our simulation against the exact answer
A nice feature of CIR is that we know the exact distribution of r_T: a scaled non-central chi-square. That lets us check that our simulation is right.


Show the code
kappa, theta, sigma, r0, T, n, M = 0.8, 0.03, 0.12, 0.08, 2.0, 400, 20_000
dt = T / n; r = np.full(M, r0)
for k in range(n):
    rp = np.maximum(r, 0)
    r = r + kappa * (theta - rp) * dt + sigma * np.sqrt(rp * dt) * rng.standard_normal(M)
c = sigma**2 * (1 - np.exp(-kappa * T)) / (4 * kappa)
df, nc = 4 * kappa * theta / sigma**2, r0 * np.exp(-kappa * T) / c
x = np.linspace(1e-5, 0.12, 400)
plt.hist(100 * np.maximum(r, 0), bins=70, density=True, color=NAVY, alpha=.35, label="simulation")
plt.plot(100 * x, stats.ncx2.pdf(x / c, df, nc) / c / 100, color=ORANGE, lw=2.2, label="exact density")
plt.xlabel("interest rate in 2 years (%)"); plt.ylabel("density"); plt.legend(); plt.show()








Figure 6: Histogram of 20,000 simulated CIR rates after 2 years (bars) against the exact non-central chi-square density (line). They agree.






Recap, step by step. Coin flips → Brownian motion (randomness) → Vasicek (+ pull toward a long-run level) → CIR (+ noise that fades near zero) → Feller condition (when zero is never reached).
Everything here assumed we know \kappa, \theta and \sigma. In the next post we ask what happens when we don’t, and that is where my research begins.

Next: Part 2 · What if we don’t know the parameters?
